Using State Measures
of Student Growth
to Inform Local Practice
(or, “Organic Isn’t Just for Veggies!”)

June, 2009

Session Learning Objectives
1. Steps to go from data to student-level
action-item
2. How and where local data fits in
3. How data quality and data use are
related

The Value of Buy-In in Arizona
1. Process was very organic, from both the top
down and the bottom up (with a little fertilizer )
2. Year-end state data was only good for the
beginning of the following year – we are
creating two types of “check point” that schools
are excited about
3. Quality means the data answers the questions
you need, and you trust it – teachers must feel
this too!

Our Process Was Very Organic and
Grass-Roots
1. Good access to data for value-added research
from previous positive relationships
• Past relationships/credibility
• Political alignment
• Collaboration with authorizer
• Participation in federal grant

Our Process Was Very Organic and
Grass-Roots
2. National and local partners focused on
understanding the “quality” landscape
• Building Charter School Quality grant, we
were approached by CO and learned about
Damian’s work in growth percentiles
• Led to Arizona State Board for Charter Schools
to redefine quality
• Led to state policymakers
taking notice

Our Process Was Very Organic and
Grass-Roots
3. Used the growth percentile data to create a best
practices report
• Highlighted how the high-growth schools got
where they are
• Focused on providing a “road-map” to other
schools to follow

Our Process Was Very Organic and
Grass-Roots
4. During research, vetted growth percentile
concept with schools and learned the best ways
to explain it
• Schools loved it
• Saw credit for growth, not starting point
• Started calling to see their own data

Our Process Was Very Organic and
Grass-Roots
5. One finding was about the importance of data-
driven decision-making
• “A-ha” moment for us
• Realized that growth percentiles could take
assessment from “end of year autopsy” to
“pre-year and mid-year diagnosis.”

Our Process Was Very Organic and
Grass-Roots
6. Became a key talking point for all of our
management team
• Goal was to change the definition of quality
in the state to “individual student level
growth” and promote “growth to standard”
instead of “one year’s growth.”
• We began to vet these ideas with state
officials, districts, and our schools.

Our Process Was Very Organic and
Grass-Roots
7. Meanwhile, we developed and marketed Best
Practice workshops
• Data-driven decision-making
• Professional Learning Communities
• Saw the growth percentile idea really appeal
to them
• Began to focus on how to develop tools for
teachers to use it more.
• Led to….

Working on Three Types of “Check Point”
(that schools are excited about)
1. Beginning of year check on growth based on end-
of-year AIMS tests
• Damian’s cool student level graphs
• Class-room level data for differentiated
instruction

Working on Three Types of “Check Point”
(that schools are excited about)
2. Online interim assessment in December
• Produce mid-point growth percentiles
• Drive instructional decisions between January
and AIMS in March

Working on Three Types of “Check Point”
(that schools are excited about)
3. Online formative assessment tool tied into PLC
concept
• Test bank/test building
• Analysis and reporting
• Professional development and
communication
• Goal is to build teacher comfort and capacity

Quality means…

1. Data answers the questions you need (i.e. you
can USE it)
• Has policy relevance
• Has classroom relevance
• Teachers can quickly understand it

Quality means…

2. You trust the data
• Reliable (would get same results again)
• Valid (measures what you want to measure)
• Transparent (we can see where the data came
from and how the results were created)

Final Thoughts

1. Need to treat the whole process like a change
management issue
2. The state/school feedback loop is critical
3. It’s All about relationships
4. It’s a GREAT time to be in education policy!
